title: Implement a food safety and quality management system in the agricultural supply chain

lessons.title: Food safety hazards and management systems
lessons.html:
Why food safety systems?

Food from farms can carry hazards that make consumers ill. Retailers, exporters and regulators require producers to show, with documents and evidence, that food is produced safely and to the agreed quality. A food safety and quality management system (FSQMS) is the structured way to do this.

Types of hazards

  • Biological: bacteria (e.g. E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria), viruses and parasites, from contaminated water, manure, unwashed hands, animals and pests.
  • Chemical: pesticide residues above the maximum residue limit (MRL), veterinary drug residues, fuel and lubricants, cleaning chemicals, mycotoxins from mouldy grain.
  • Physical: glass, metal, stones, wood splinters, jewellery, plastic.
  • Allergens: relevant mainly in processing.

Common systems and standards

  • Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) schemes for primary production, such as SA-GAP (locally) and GLOBALG.A.P. (widely required for export and by major retailers).
  • HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points), the internationally recognised method for analysing and controlling hazards, mainly in packhouses and processing.
  • ISO 22000 and FSSC 22000, and BRCGS, for processors and packers.
  • Customer-specific codes from retailers.

Legal framework

Food safety in South Africa is regulated under laws including the Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972 and, for meat, the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Agricultural remedies must be registered under Act 36 of 1947 and used according to the label. Export products must meet the importing country's requirements, checked through official export certification.

The seven HACCP principles

  1. Conduct a hazard analysis.
  2. Determine critical control points (CCPs).
  3. Set critical limits.
  4. Establish monitoring procedures.
  5. Establish corrective actions.
  6. Establish verification procedures.
  7. Keep records and documentation.

lessons.title: Implementing the system on farm and in the packhouse
lessons.html:
Prerequisite programmes

Before HACCP or GAP can work, basic controls must be in place:

  • Personal hygiene: handwashing stations with soap, water and paper towels; toilets near fields; rules on jewellery, eating, smoking and illness reporting.
  • Water management: risk assessment and testing of water used for irrigation, spraying and washing.
  • Pest control: rodent bait stations mapped and checked in stores and packhouses; birds kept out.
  • Cleaning and sanitation: schedules for crates, equipment and packing surfaces, with approved chemicals.
  • Plant protection products: only registered products, applied by trained operators per label; spray records; pre-harvest intervals observed.
  • Glass and hard plastic policy: covered lights, registers of breakable items.
  • Training of all workers, with attendance records.
  • Supplier control: approved suppliers for packaging, chemicals and seed.

Implementation steps

  1. Appoint a food safety team and leader with management support.
  2. Map the process from field to dispatch.
  3. Carry out the hazard analysis and risk assessments.
  4. Write procedures, work instructions and record sheets.
  5. Train workers and supervisors.
  6. Monitor CCPs and prerequisites, record results and take corrective action when limits are exceeded.
  7. Conduct internal audits and management reviews.
  8. Prepare for the external audit and close out non-conformances.

Traceability and recall

Each lot must be traceable one step back (field, block, supplier) and one step forward (customer). Use lot numbers on labels and dispatch records. Test a mock recall regularly to confirm you can trace a lot quickly.

Quality management

Quality covers specifications such as size, colour, Brix, defects and packaging. Use sampling plans, inspection checklists and calibrated scales and instruments. Record rejections and analyse causes.

Managing non-conformances

When something goes wrong, record it, contain affected product, find the root cause, correct it and verify that the fix worked.

Key points

  • Hazards are biological, chemical, physical and allergenic.
  • GAP schemes and HACCP are the core systems in agricultural supply chains.
  • Prerequisites such as hygiene, water, pest control and cleaning come first.
  • Monitor, record and correct; audit internally and externally.
  • Traceability and mock recalls protect customers and the business.
